children: New frontiers are emerging on the battlefield, with countries increasingly investing in laser weapons, space warfare and even humanoid robots.
Once a staple of science fiction,
are now a military reality for the U.S.

For instance, the U.S. used a high-energy laser weapon system for the first time to down suspicious drones near the Mexico border. The U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa have used Boeing's
Compact Laser Weapon System to combat drones overseas.
This month, the U.S. Army awarded its first production contract for high-energy laser weapon systems to AeroVironment
and nLight secured contracts for the Joint Laser Weapon System, which will be capable of downing drones and cruise missiles.

"High-energy lasers and high-power microwaves are becoming essential elements of naval warfare," Daryl Caudle, Chief of Naval Operations, wrote in a recent memo. "The question is no longer whether these systems work – it is how quickly we can field them across the fleet."
Elsewhere, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems delivered the Iron Beam to the Israel Defense Forces last year – the world's first combat deployment of a high-power laser-based aerial interception system.

is now a strategic focus for countries. "Space is increasingly viewed as a critical operating domain, underpinning communications, navigation, and full-spectrum combat capabilities – with the next peer-to-peer conflict involving the U.S. and its allies likely to extend into space," Goldman Sachs analysts observed recently.

President Trump's Golden Dome program envisions one space-based layer that includes sensors and intercept capabilities, as well as three land-based layers. The Pentagon is targeting to conduct the Golden Dome's first major test in H2 2028.

This week, the U.S. Space Command practiced "orbital dogfighting" – maneuvering satellites in proximity to one another in a simulated conflict environment. Chinese satellites reportedly demonstrated this capability in 2024.

The Space Force has forecast the U.S. satellite fleet growing from about 7K in 2025 to ~30K in 2040, while China's fleet is seen expanding from 1.9K in 2025 to ~21K in 2040. To maintain its edge, the agency called for deepening partnerships with commercial space companies.
have been grabbing headlines, with China touting its advances at the recent World Humanoid
Now Beijing is ramping up research into humanoids' military uses and planning for their eventual deployment in the battlefield,
reported, citing government records. To note, there is no evidence that China deployed an armed humanoid with an operational military unit.

The U.S. military is also testing humanoid robots, but this is limited to handling weapons and not firing them. The Army also has an ongoing contest for humanoid technology with militarized capabilities.

For now, humanoid robots still have a long way to go before they can be deployed in the battlefield. Sam Bresnick, research fellow at Georgetown University Center for Security and Emerging Technology, believes it could take 5-10 years.

title: Laser weapons, space dogfights, and humanoid robots: The future of the battlefield
